title: Energy Analysis of Closed Systems
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 4
summary:
This chapter applies the first law to a **closed system** — fixed mass, no flow across the boundary. The new piece of physics is **moving-boundary work** (boundary work), the work done as a gas expands or is compressed by a piston: $W_b = \int_1^2 P\,dV$. Geometrically it is the **area under the process path on a $P\text{-}V$ diagram**, which is why the *path* matters, not just the endpoints — different routes between the same two states do different amounts of work.

That integral collapses into clean formulas for the standard idealized processes. **Constant volume** (isochoric): no boundary movement, so $W_b = 0$. **Constant pressure** (isobaric): $W_b = P(V_2 - V_1)$. **Isothermal** expansion of an ideal gas: $W_b = mRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$. The general **polytropic** process $PV^n = \text{const}$ covers the rest, with $W_b = (P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)/(1-n)$ for $n \ne 1$. Knowing which case you're in turns a calculus problem into arithmetic.

The **closed-system energy balance** is $Q - W = \Delta U\,(+\Delta KE + \Delta PE)$. Drop the kinetic and potential terms for a stationary system and you get the everyday form $Q - W_b = \Delta U$. A neat special case: for a **constant-pressure** process with only boundary work, the $W_b$ and $PV$ terms combine so that $Q = \Delta H$ — heat equals the enthalpy change. That's why enthalpy is so handy.

To evaluate $\Delta U$ and $\Delta H$ you use **specific heats**: $c_v = (\partial u/\partial T)_v$ and $c_p = (\partial h/\partial T)_p$. For an **ideal gas**, $u$ and $h$ depend on temperature alone, giving the simple $\Delta u = c_v\,\Delta T$ and $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$, with $c_p = c_v + R$ and $k = c_p/c_v$. For **solids and liquids** (incompressible), $c_p \approx c_v = c$, so $\Delta u = c\,\Delta T$.

The workflow: identify the process (which sets the work formula), evaluate the property changes (table or specific-heat relation), and close the energy balance for the unknown.

equations.name: Boundary work (general)
equations.useWhen: A closed system's boundary moves (a piston). This is the master form — specialize it to the process below rather than integrating from scratch.
equations.note: Path-dependent: different processes between the same end states give different $W_b$.

equations.name: Boundary work — constant volume
equations.useWhen: Rigid tank / clamped piston — the volume can't change, so no boundary work is done regardless of pressure.

equations.name: Boundary work — constant pressure
equations.useWhen: A piston free to move under a fixed weight/atmosphere, so pressure stays constant as volume changes (e.g. heating gas under a loaded piston).
equations.note: For this case with only boundary work, $Q = \Delta H$.

equations.name: Boundary work — isothermal ideal gas
equations.useWhen: An ideal gas expands or is compressed at constant temperature ($PV = \text{const}$). Since $\Delta U = 0$ here, $Q = W_b$.
equations.note: Use $V_2/V_1 = P_1/P_2$ to swap the volume ratio for a pressure ratio.

equations.name: Boundary work — polytropic
equations.useWhen: A process follows $PV^n = \text{const}$ with $n \ne 1$. Covers most real compressions/expansions; for $n = 1$ use the isothermal log form instead.
equations.note: Special cases: $n=0$ constant pressure, $n=1$ isothermal, $n=k$ isentropic, $n \to \infty$ constant volume.

equations.name: Closed-system energy balance
equations.useWhen: Any closed-system process. Pick the reduced form that matches your case (rigid, constant-pressure, etc.).

equations.name: Ideal-gas internal energy & enthalpy
equations.latex: \Delta u = c_v\,\Delta T, \qquad \Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T
equations.useWhen: Finding internal-energy or enthalpy changes of an ideal gas. $u$ and $h$ depend on temperature only, so these hold for *any* process (not just constant V or P).
equations.note: Use average specific heats over the temperature range, or table values $u(T), h(T)$ for high accuracy.

equations.name: Incompressible substance (solids & liquids)
equations.latex: \Delta u = c\,\Delta T, \qquad \Delta h = c\,\Delta T + v\,\Delta P
equations.useWhen: Heating/cooling solids or liquids, where volume barely changes. The $v\,\Delta P$ term in $\Delta h$ is often negligible.
equations.note: A single specific heat $c$ suffices because $c_p \approx c_v$ for incompressible substances.

glossary.definition: A fixed quantity of matter; energy may cross the boundary but mass cannot. Also called a control mass.
Work done as a system boundary moves, $W_b = \int P\,dV$; the area under the process path on a $P$-$V$ diagram.
A plot of pressure vs. volume; the area under a quasi-equilibrium process path equals the boundary work.
A process at fixed volume; $W_b = 0$ and $Q = \Delta U$.
A process at fixed pressure; $W_b = P\,\Delta V$ and $Q = \Delta H$ (boundary work only).
A constant-temperature process; for an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W_b$.
A process obeying $PV^n = \text{const}$. The exponent $n$ selects the case (0, 1, k, ∞).
$c_v = (\partial u/\partial T)_v$ — energy to raise unit mass by one degree at constant volume.
$c_p = (\partial h/\partial T)_p$ — energy to raise unit mass by one degree at constant pressure. For ideal gas, $c_p = c_v + R$.
$k = c_p/c_v$; about 1.4 for air. Governs isentropic relations (Ch 7).
A substance whose specific volume is essentially constant (solids, liquids); then $c_p \approx c_v = c$.

tips: **Find the process first, then the work.** "Rigid" → $W_b=0$; "piston free under constant weight" → $W_b = P\,\Delta V$; "$PV^n$" → polytropic formula. The process keyword tells you which one.
**$\Delta u = c_v\Delta T$ and $\Delta h = c_p\Delta T$ hold for an ideal gas in ANY process** — not only constant-V or constant-P. A common misconception is to restrict them.
**Constant-pressure shortcut:** with only boundary work, $Q = \Delta H$. You can skip computing $W_b$ separately and read enthalpy from the tables.
**Boundary work is path-dependent; $\Delta U$ is not.** $U$ is a property (endpoints only); $W$ and $Q$ depend on the route taken.
**Watch the sign of work in the balance.** Expansion does work *by* the system (positive $W$, lowers $U$); compression does work *on* it (negative $W$).
**Pick good specific-heat values.** Over a large temperature span use average $c$ values or the $u(T)/h(T)$ tables rather than room-temperature constants.
